faqs.question: What is a simple Diwali greeting for a 3-year-old?
faqs.answer: Say it rather than write it: three to eight words about something the child can see, such as "One diya for you, one for me. Happy Diwali!" Children of 4–5 use broad words like "happy" well before specific ones, so skip "prosperity" and "blessings" at this age.

faqs.question: How many words should a Diwali message to a child have?
faqs.answer: About 3–8 spoken words under age 5, 6–10 words at 5–7, around 20 words at 8–10 and 30–40 words from 11. ASER 2024 found only 23.4% of Std III children in government schools could read a Std II text, so shorter is safer at every age.

faqs.question: What should a teacher write to students for Diwali?
faqs.answer: One line for the whole class and, where time allows, a named line for each child that mentions something from this term. Send it in the last class before the school's Diwali break, which for Diwali on Friday 29 October 2027 usually means Wednesday 27 or Thursday 28 October.

faqs.question: What can my child write in a Diwali card for grandparents?
faqs.answer: Whatever they can spell without help: "Diya for Dadi" at 5, one sentence at 7, and two sentences with a real detail, such as which sweet they helped make, at 9 or 10. Let the child choose the line so it sounds like them.

faqs.question: Should a Diwali greeting for kids mention Lakshmi or the puja?
faqs.answer: Only if your family does the puja and the child takes part in it. For a class or a mixed-faith group, greetings built on diyas, rangoli, sweets and family time include every child without asking anyone to share a ritual.

faqs.question: How do I wish a child in my class who does not celebrate Diwali?
faqs.answer: Wish the whole class a happy Diwali and a happy holiday in the same line, so the holiday, the lights and the sweets are shared even when the puja is not. Avoid singling the child out or asking them to explain why they do not celebrate.

faqs.question: Is it okay to mention firecrackers in a Diwali wish for kids?
faqs.answer: Leave them out, or mention them only with distance and adults in charge. In a 2023–2024 study of 67 Diwali firecracker eye injuries in Central and Western India, 62.7% of patients were children and 34.3% were bystanders.

faqs.question: Can my 10-year-old send Diwali wishes on WhatsApp?
faqs.answer: Not from their own account in most of India: WhatsApp's terms require users to be at least 13, with parent-managed accounts below that age only where available. Let the child dictate or type the greeting and send it from a parent's phone.

faqs.question: When are Diwali and Bhai Dooj in 2027?
faqs.answer: Diwali (Lakshmi Puja) is on Friday 29 October 2027 and Bhai Dooj on Sunday 31 October 2027. A child's Bhai Dooj line for a sibling can go out that Sunday morning.

faqs.question: Can a child open the SubhSandesh Diwali card on a tablet?
faqs.answer: Yes. The /happy-diwali page fits one screen on phones, tablets and laptops and every interaction is a single tap, and 48.4% of SubhSandesh page views are already on a touch device. Its crackers are drawn by the page, with no noise or smoke.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Diwali Greetings for Kids, Graded by Age: To Them and From Them

Diwali greetings for kids work when they match what the child can say, read or write: one spoken line under age 5, one sentence with their name at 5–7, two sentences with a real detail at 8–10, and a short note from 11. On SubhSandesh, 48.4% of all page views happen on a touch device and a shared page is opened 11.1 times on average, so a greeting for a child should work with one tap and survive replays.

Below are original lines in two directions, to children and by children, graded by age. Diwali 2027 falls on Friday 29 October, with Bhai Dooj on Sunday 31 October.

## What makes a Diwali greeting fit a child's age?

A child-fit greeting uses words the child already owns and is short enough to read, or hear, in one go. A line a seven-year-old cannot decode gets read to them, and stops being theirs.

Two pieces of evidence set the grading. In a study of 123 children aged 4 to 11, [Grosse and colleagues (Affective Science, 2021)](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9382957) found that older children produce more emotion words, and that broad words such as "happy" and "sad" arrive earlier than specific ones.

The youngest group, aged 4–5, tended to lump all positive feelings together. So "happy" lands with a four-year-old; "blessed" and "prosperous" do not. Reading is the second constraint, in the table below.

## Diwali greetings for kids, from the adults in their life

Each band gives length, delivery, one thing to include, and lines. Swap in the child's name.

### Ages 2–4: one spoken line

Length: three to eight words, said aloud. Delivery: in person or on a video call, since the child cannot read it. Include: something they can see or touch right now.

- "One diya for you, one for me. Happy Diwali, Chotu!"
- "Look, the whole street switched on for you!"
- "Happy Diwali, my little laddoo inspector."

### Ages 5–7: one sentence with their name

Length: six to ten words. Delivery: a card they can sound out with you. Include: their name and one thing they did.

- "Happy Diwali, Riya! Your diya was the first one lit this year."
- "Nani is keeping the biggest besan laddoo aside for you."
- "Your rangoli made our door look happy. Happy Diwali!"

### Ages 8–10: two sentences and one real detail

Length: about 20 words. Delivery: a handwritten card or a message on a parent's phone. Include: a specific thing you noticed, since children this age can hold words like "proud" and "patient".

- "Happy Diwali, Kabir. I noticed how patiently you waited your turn at the puja, and I was proud of you."
- "This Diwali you shared your sweets box with the watchman's son without being asked. Keep that habit for every festival."
- "Dada's Diwali riddle: I am made of clay, I drink oil, and I only work at night. Call me with the answer!"

### Ages 11–13: a short note they might keep

Length: 30–40 words. Delivery: a card in their room, or a message on the family phone. Include: how they have changed since last Diwali.

- "Happy Diwali, Meher. Next year you'll probably find this message embarrassing; keep it anyway."
- "Twelve Diwalis now. You went from being scared of the dark to being the one who lights the diyas for everyone else."
- "Diwali is about light finding its way into a house. You do that for ours more than you know."

## Diwali greetings by kids: lines a child can write themselves

Greetings by children must be copyable without help, so this grading runs on spelling, not vocabulary. Let the child pick the line, or it reads like homework.

### Age 5–6: three or four words plus a drawing

- "Diya for Dadi"
- "Happy Diwali Nana. Love, Anu"
- "Me + Papa + diya = Diwali"
- नानी, मेरा दीया आपके लिए जला है। (Nani, mera diya aapke liye jala hai. — "Nani, my diya is lit for you.") Best said on the phone; a parent can write it.

### Age 7–8: one sentence they can spell

- "Happy Diwali, Ma'am. I drew this diya for your table."
- "Happy Diwali, Nana. Come and see my rangoli before it gets swept."
- "Happy Diwali, Aarav. Let's swap sweets after the holiday."

### Age 9–10: two sentences with a detail

- "Dear Dadi, Happy Diwali! I helped Mumma make karanjis this year and only two broke."
- "Dear Sir, Happy Diwali. You explained fractions three times and never got cross."
- "Didi, Happy Bhai Dooj! My half of the kaju katli is yours, just this once."

### Age 11–13: a short note in their own voice

- "Dear Ma'am, Happy Diwali. Yours is the only class where I forget to watch the clock."
- "Nana, Happy Diwali from Pune. The diyas here are fine, but none of them are as crooked as yours, and I miss that."
- "Happy Diwali to everyone in 7B, including the people who still owe me an eraser."

## Diwali greetings for students: a teacher's lines before the break

With Diwali on Friday 29 October 2027, a teacher's greeting goes out in the last class before the school's own break, often Wednesday 27 or Thursday 28 October, via the class diary or parents' group. One class line covers 40 children; a named line takes two minutes and is the one families keep.

- Whole class: "Happy Diwali, Class 4C. Help at home, eat one sweet too many, and bring back one story to tell us."
- Mixed-faith class: "Happy Diwali to everyone who celebrates, and a happy holiday to all of you. Enjoy the lights on your street."
- A child who worked hard this term: "Happy Diwali, Ishaan. Your reading got much stronger this term; read one page aloud to your family over the holiday."
- A board-exam class: "Happy Diwali, Class 10. Rest for two days without guilt. The syllabus will still be here after the break."

## Greeting length by age, against what Indian children can read

The comparison below sets the length guide from this page against reading levels measured by [ASER 2024's national findings](https://asercentre.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/ASER-2024-National-findings.pdf), a 2025 report on a rural household survey of 649,491 children run by Pratham. ASER tests reading one-on-one in the child's own language, so English-medium reading may differ.

| Age (class) | Greeting length to aim for | ASER 2024 reading result | Best way to deliver it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2–4 (pre-school) | 3–8 words, spoken | Not tested: ASER reading starts at age 5 | Said in person or on a video call |
| 5–7 (Std I–II) | 6–10 words, one sentence | Not in the national summary; read it together | Card sounded out with an adult |
| 8–10 (Std III–V) | About 20 words, two sentences | Std III government schools 23.4%; Std V 44.8% (private 59.3%) read a Std II text | Handwritten card or a parent's phone |
| 11–13 (Std VI–VIII) | 30–40 words, a short note | Std VIII government schools 67.5% | Card, or the family phone until 13 |

The takeaway: fewer than a quarter of Std III children in government schools read a Std II story, so at eight even a two-sentence greeting may be read aloud by an adult. Start each band at its shortest.

## Crackers in a child's greeting: what 67 eye-injury cases say

Keep firecrackers out of greetings written for children, and never make bursting them the wish. A [multicentre study in the Indian Journal of Ophthalmology (2026)](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13674918) followed 67 people treated for firecracker eye injuries over the 2023 and 2024 Diwali seasons in Central and Western India: 62.7% were children, the median age was 14, and 34.3% were hurt as bystanders rather than while lighting anything.

That bystander figure matters most: a child watching from the gate is not automatically safe. A greeting that steers toward diyas, rangoli and sweets does more than one promising "lots of crackers". If crackers come up, frame them around distance and adults:

- "Happy Diwali! The best seat for the night sky is behind a grown-up, with your hands in your pockets."
- "A rangoli can't burn you and a diya story can't scare the dog. Happy, safe Diwali!"

## Sending a child's greeting to someone far away

Children under 13 should send through a parent. [WhatsApp's terms of service](https://www.whatsapp.com/legal/terms-of-service) require users to be at least 13 to have their own account, and a parent-managed account below that age is offered only in some countries, so for most Indian families the greeting goes from a parent's phone.

For a grandparent or cousin in another city, SubhSandesh's [interactive Diwali card with a family mode](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-diwali) suits a child's attention span: they light a diya at the door, light a row of wish diyas, colour a rangoli until initials glow, and write a word with a sparkler, all with a single tap. Its crackers are drawn, with no noise or smoke, and it takes about five minutes to build.

A parent types the child's lines into the wish diyas and the letter, then sends the private link, which opens in any browser with no app. Since 38.5% of SubhSandesh creators password-protect a page before sharing, adding one for a page carrying a child's photos is a normal step.

For a grandparent who wants to play something back, [a photo jigsaw that reveals a letter piece by piece](https://subhsandesh.in/photo-puzzle) works the other way round: the child solves it, and each placed piece shows one line from Dada or Nani. It suits a child who already enjoys simple jigsaws.

## When a screen greeting is the wrong one for a child

Under about age 3, a screen greeting is mostly for the parents. Send the link to the adults and save the words for a hug.

A handwritten card also beats a link for any child old enough to write one. The wobbly letters are the point.

48.3% of SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone, where a link sinks under forwarded messages, while a paper card can sit on Nani's shelf until next Diwali. Use the link for distance, and the card for everyone in reach.

## Sources

- Grosse G. et al. "Let's Talk About Emotions: the Development of Children's Emotion Vocabulary from 4 to 11 Years of Age." Affective Science, 16 April 2021.
- ASER Centre / Pratham. "ASER 2024 National findings." 2025 (PDF dated 13 February 2025).
- Bhasin P. et al. "Firecracker-related ocular injuries during the Diwali festival." Indian Journal of Ophthalmology, 24 August 2026.
- WhatsApp LLC. "WhatsApp Terms of Service", Age section, read 22 October 2026.

structuralLimitations: No Diwali usage data exists (/happy-diwali is new); first-party lines are platform-wide (touch-device share, views per page, phone opens, password use). No per-age or per-recipient data exists.
The word-length bands per age are this post's own guide, informed by ASER 2024 and Grosse et al. 2021; neither source prescribes greeting lengths, and the body labels them as a guide.

ASER tests reading in the child's own language in rural households; English-medium and urban reading may differ, and the body says so. ASER's national summary gives no Std I–II reading figure, so the 5–7 row says 'not in the national summary'.
Grosse et al. studied German-speaking children; the finding used (broad emotion words before specific ones) is applied to Indian English and Hindi greetings by analogy.
Firecracker study is CC BY-NC-ND: cited and linked only; no text or table reproduced. n = 67 at three centres in Central/Western India, not national.

NIPUN Bharat oral-reading-fluency benchmarks were considered but both official PDFs (ncert.nic.in, nipunbharat.education.gov.in) are image-only scans that could not be text-verified, so they are not cited.

SubhSandesh holds no data on recipients' ages or on greetings to children, so no first-party column fits without inventing one; the first-party numbers (48.4% touch-device views, 11.1 views per page, 48.3% phone opens, 38.5% password use) sit in the prose instead. auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page in the measured top 10 that grades Diwali greetings for kids by age in both directions and ties the lengths to ASER 2024 reading results, child emotion-vocabulary research and a 2026 Diwali eye-injury study, while the ranking pages are image boards, videos and one 2026-dated list (printsheetlab) with recipient sections but no age reasoning. Domain authority is far below Pinterest and YouTube, the SERP is visual-heavy, and printsheetlab is a strong text incumbent, so expect months, not weeks; the first-party data says nothing specific about children.
